summary:
Vesta: an AI companion that cares for astronauts’ body and mind

On long-duration missions, the crew’s mental state is as mission-critical as their vital signs, yet it is still measured with questionnaires that are easy to skip. Vesta closes that gap.

A wearable streams temperature, heart rate and SpO₂ in real time, with automatic alerts. In parallel, Vesta holds a short, hands-free conversation in natural language: no yes-or-no prompts, no buttons. Its AI interprets what the astronaut says and maps it to PANAS, a scientifically established psychological scale, turning a five-question chat into a full affect profile that the astronaut confirms.

Vesta adapts to each individual: it learns the astronaut’s personal baseline, detects meaningful deviations and explains them with NASA evidence, escalating to the flight surgeon when needed. Every session and correction feeds a mission dataset designed to train future models.

Built for deep space, it keeps running without contact with Earth, falling back from cloud AI to an onboard local model, while critical alerts always remain deterministic.
details:
What it does and how it works

Vesta monitors an astronaut’s physical and mental health together. A wearable built on an ESP8266 with an LM35 temperature sensor and a MAX30102 heart-rate and SpO₂ sensor sends vital signs every second over MQTT to a live dashboard, where deterministic rules raise alerts at two levels. Alongside it, Vesta, a hands-free voice assistant, replaces the traditional questionnaire with a short conversation. It asks open questions such as “How’s your energy today?” and the astronaut answers in their own words. A classifier maps each answer to the 20 feelings of PANAS (Positive and Negative Affect Schedule), an established psychological scale, so a single answer like “a bit tired, but really proud of the team” fills in several feelings at once. Feelings that were not mentioned are estimated and clearly marked. Before anything is saved, Vesta shows what it understood and the astronaut confirms or corrects it. The result is then compared with the astronaut’s own baseline, explained in plain language with NASA evidence, and flagged for the flight surgeon when the change is large.

Benefits

A daily check-in takes about a minute of conversation instead of a 20-item form, so astronauts are far more likely to keep doing it. Physical and mental health are shown side by side but never merged into a misleading “fit/unfit” score. Because Vesta compares each person with themselves, it can detect changes early, before they become problems. It also reduces the load on ground teams: Vesta supports the astronaut on board and escalates only what matters.

Expected impact

On missions to the Moon and Mars, round-trip communication delays of up to about 40 minutes mean crews will need health support that works on board. Vesta addresses gaps identified in NASA’s Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC) Evidence Report, namely personalized medicine and computer-based decision support for autonomous crews. Every check-in, correction and piece of feedback is logged as a mission dataset, which can become the foundation for validated, crew-specific mental health models. The same approach could also help people in other isolated and confined settings, such as Antarctic stations, submarines and remote work sites.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

The hardware is an ESP8266 (NodeMCU) with LM35 and MAX30102 sensors, programmed in Arduino C++. Data travels over MQTT through Eclipse Mosquitto. The backend is written in Java 21 with Spring Boot and handles PANAS scoring, the answer classifier, baseline analysis, AI guardrails and the mission log; Python is used for the data collector and the simulator. The web interface uses PHP, HTML, JavaScript and MQTT.js, with the Web Speech API for hands-free voice, and data is stored in MariaDB/MySQL. For the explanations, Vesta uses Claude in the cloud, Ollama with Llama 3.2 as an on-board local model, and a fixed template as the final fallback, all grounded in retrieved NASA evidence. The whole system runs on a single computer with Docker Compose. The demo videos were made with Remotion and Piper TTS synthetic voices.

What makes it creative

Vesta turns a standard psychological questionnaire into a natural conversation without losing the scientific scale underneath. It treats the astronaut as a partner rather than a subject, because they see, correct and confirm their own result. Its AI degrades gracefully from the cloud to an on-board model to a template, so the crew is never left without an answer. It also brings live vital signs and mental state into one view without mixing them into a single score.

Factors our team considered
Safety came first: critical alerts always come from deterministic rules, and the AI can raise their severity but never lower or silence them. The system is offline-first, so its essential functions do not depend on Earth or the internet, and it is resilient: it restarts on its own after a power cut, stores data durably, and reports a missing sensor as “missing” rather than “normal”. We were careful about scientific honesty: estimated feelings are labeled, and the quick check-in is presented as an estimate, not a diagnosis. We also considered ethics and privacy, keeping the astronaut in control of their own data and limiting suggestions to an approved list of actions. Finally, we designed for human factors, with short, friendly, hands-free interactions that fit into a busy mission schedule.
